title: Cushing syndrome, high-normal ACTH, suppressed by high- (not low-) dose dexamethasone: pituitary adenoma (Cushing disease)
vignette: A 56-year-old woman comes to the office due to progressive weight gain and fatigue over the last 4 months. She also has had increasing difficulty in lifting heavy objects and climbing stairs. The patient has moderate, persistent bronchial asthma for which she uses inhaled corticosteroids and beta-2 agonists. Family history is significant for colon cancer in her father. Blood pressure is 160/90 mm Hg and pulse is 80/min. On physical examination, there is symmetric proximal muscle weakness of the upper and lower extremities. Fasting plasma glucose level is 135 mg/dL and 24-hour urinary cortisol is increased. Further evaluation reveals that high-dose, but not low-dose, dexamethasone suppresses serum cortisol levels. Serum ACTH levels are high-normal. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's symptoms?

clues.note: Elevated 24-hour urinary free cortisol confirms endogenous CORTISOL EXCESS (Cushing syndrome).

clues.text: high-dose, but not low-dose, dexamethasone suppresses serum cortisol levels
clues.note: Failure to suppress with LOW-dose but suppression with HIGH-dose dexamethasone is the pattern of a pituitary ACTH-secreting adenoma (Cushing disease).
A non-suppressed (high/normal) ACTH indicates ACTH-DEPENDENT Cushing syndrome - pituitary or ectopic - not an adrenal source.

whatMatters: Cushing syndrome (high urinary cortisol) that is ACTH-DEPENDENT (high-normal ACTH) and SUPPRESSES with HIGH-dose but NOT low-dose dexamethasone = an ACTH-secreting PITUITARY ADENOMA (Cushing DISEASE) - the most common cause of endogenous Cushing syndrome. Answer D.
strategy: Work the algorithm: confirm hypercortisolism (high urinary cortisol, not suppressed by low-dose dexamethasone), then use ACTH to split dependent vs independent - high/normal ACTH = ACTH-dependent. High-dose dexamethasone SUPPRESSION indicates a PITUITARY source. Reject adrenal adenoma/carcinoma (ACTH-independent -> LOW/suppressed ACTH), exogenous glucocorticoids (ACTH suppressed; inhaled steroids rarely cause it), and ectopic ACTH (small cell lung cancer) - NOT suppressed by high-dose dexamethasone.

eliminations.label: Adrenal adenoma - ACTH-independent (low ACTH)
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: an autonomously cortisol-secreting adrenal tumor. ❌ WHY IT FAILS: it is ACTH-INDEPENDENT, so ACTH would be SUPPRESSED (low), not high-normal; cortisol wouldn't suppress with dexamethasone. ✅ Correct if: hypercortisolism with a suppressed ACTH.

eliminations.label: Adrenal carcinoma - ACTH-independent
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: an adrenocortical malignancy autonomously making cortisol (often with androgens). ❌ WHY IT FAILS: also ACTH-INDEPENDENT (low ACTH); doesn't fit high-normal ACTH. ✅ Correct if: rapid virilizing hypercortisolism with a suppressed ACTH.

eliminations.label: Exogenous glucocorticoids - suppressed ACTH
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: iatrogenic Cushing from steroid intake. ❌ WHY IT FAILS: exogenous steroids SUPPRESS ACTH and cortisol; inhaled corticosteroids rarely cause systemic Cushing, and here urinary cortisol is high with non-suppressed ACTH. ✅ Correct if: systemic steroid use with low ACTH/low endogenous cortisol.

eliminations.label: Small cell lung cancer - ectopic ACTH (no high-dose suppression)
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: ectopic ACTH production (paraneoplastic). ❌ WHY IT FAILS: ectopic ACTH is NOT suppressed by high-dose dexamethasone (this patient DID suppress), and often causes very high ACTH with hyperpigmentation/hypokalemia. ✅ Correct if: hypercortisolism not suppressed by high-dose dexamethasone.

reasoning: Increased urinary cortisol confirms Cushing syndrome
High-normal ACTH indicates ACTH-dependent disease (pituitary or ectopic)
Suppression with high-dose (but not low-dose) dexamethasone points to a pituitary source
-> ACTH-secreting pituitary adenoma (Cushing disease); answer D
mechanism: CUSHING SYNDROME is chronic cortisol excess (weight gain, proximal muscle weakness, hypertension, hyperglycemia, striae, easy bruising). Diagnosis proceeds in two steps. FIRST, confirm hypercortisolism with screening tests (elevated 24-hour urinary free cortisol; failure of LOW-DOSE dexamethasone to suppress cortisol; late-night salivary cortisol). SECOND, determine the cause using serum ACTH: if ACTH is LOW/SUPPRESSED, the source is ACTH-INDEPENDENT (adrenal adenoma/carcinoma/hyperplasia or exogenous steroids); if ACTH is HIGH or inappropriately NORMAL, it is ACTH-DEPENDENT (pituitary 'Cushing DISEASE' or ectopic ACTH). To distinguish pituitary from ectopic, a HIGH-DOSE dexamethasone suppression test is used: a corticotroph PITUITARY ADENOMA retains partial negative feedback and SUPPRESSES cortisol with high-dose dexamethasone, whereas ECTOPIC ACTH (e.g., small cell lung cancer) does NOT suppress. This patient has elevated urinary cortisol, high-normal ACTH, and suppression with high- (but not low-) dose dexamethasone - the signature of an ACTH-secreting PITUITARY ADENOMA (the most common cause of endogenous Cushing syndrome). The distractors are adrenal (ACTH-independent, low ACTH), exogenous steroids (low ACTH), and ectopic ACTH (no high-dose suppression).

difficulty.label: 🧠 Knowledge
difficulty.text: First Aid Endo > Cushing syndrome workup: screen (urinary free cortisol, low-dose dexamethasone, late-night salivary cortisol); ACTH separates dependent (pituitary/ectopic) vs independent (adrenal/exogenous, low ACTH); high-dose dexamethasone suppresses pituitary (Cushing disease) but not ectopic ACTH.

difficulty.label: 📖 Comprehension
difficulty.text: High-normal ACTH + high-dose (not low-dose) suppression = pituitary adenoma (Cushing disease).

difficulty.label: 🔤 Vocab
difficulty.text: Unsure on Cushing syndrome/disease, ACTH-dependent vs independent, dexamethasone suppression tests, or ectopic ACTH? Tell me which.

difficulty.label: 🨤 Distractor
difficulty.text: Adrenal/exogenous = LOW ACTH (independent); ectopic ACTH (SCLC) does NOT suppress with high-dose dexamethasone.

difficulty.label: 🗒️ Other
difficulty.text: Bank: ACTH high-normal + suppresses with high-dose dexamethasone = pituitary (Cushing disease); ectopic = no suppression.

keywords.back: No suppression (even high-dose); e.g., small cell lung cancer

firstAid.detail: Endo: pituitary ACTH adenoma; high-dose dexamethasone suppresses.
Endo > adrenal (low ACTH), ectopic (no suppression), exogenous.
Endo > dependent vs independent; pituitary vs ectopic.

memoryHook: High-normal ACTH that still bows to HIGH-dose dexamethasone = a pituitary adenoma keeping a little feedback (Cushing disease); ectopic tumors ignore the dexamethasone entirely.
